en: The Kāśyapaparivarta Sūtra. Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain, together with a great saṅgha of monks—eight thousand monks and sixteen [thousand bodhisattvas].
There were thousands of bodhisattvas who had gathered from various buddha-fields, all bound by only one more birth before attaining unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Mahākāśyapa:
"What are the four? Namely, they are those who lack respect for the Dharma and for the preacher of the Dharma."
And they become [obstacles] to the Dharma;

he practices the "teacher's fist" regarding the Dharma and creates an obstruction to the Dharma for those persons who desire the Dharma; he diverts their interest, distracts them, and does not teach it.
He conceals [his faults],
and he becomes one who is full of self-conceit, exalting himself and disparaging others.
Kāśyapa, these four qualities lead to the decline of a bodhisattva’s wisdom.
In this regard, the following is said:
He is disrespectful toward the Dharma-preacher and takes delight in stinginess regarding the teachings;
he practices the "teacher's fist" with respect to the Dharma.
Seeking his own gain, he creates obstacles for those who seek the Dharma;
disparaging and reviling them in various ways, he does not teach the Dharma praised by the Jinas.
Constantly intent on self-exaltation and delighting in disparaging others—
these four qualities are declared by the Victor to be the characteristics of the indolent.
For the sake of abandoning [unwholesome] wisdom,
one should abandon these four factors and cultivate the four supreme dharmas spoken by the Victor.

KP.2. Kāśyapa, there are these four qualities that lead to a bodhisattva’s great wisdom. What are the four? That he is respectful toward the Dharma and the teacher of the Dharma; and that he extensively elucidates to others the teachings exactly as they have been heard and exactly as they have been mastered.
With a mind free from worldly desire, he does not expect anything in return... [KP.3] ...and he does not utter dispraise, ill-repute, or slanderous words concerning sentient beings;
nor does he deal with others through deceit and guile, but rather through his noble resolve (*adhyāśaya*).
Kāśyapa, the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) becomes deluded in one who is possessed of these four qualities.
Regarding this, it is said:
They do not perform what is to be done for the teacher who is worthy of offerings;
they instill remorse in others regarding those beings who are established in awakening.
They speak dispraise and infamy of them, saying that they act through deceit, guile, trickery,
and with a mind intent on destruction.
These dharmas are to be cultivated...
[in] delusion... the mind [should be directed] toward the supreme enlightenment of a Buddha; therefore, while practicing these... one should [proceed].
Practicing the supreme and foremost Dharma for a very long time,
he touched the supreme and foremost state and attained tranquility.

KP.4: Kāśyapa, for a bodhisattva endowed with four qualities, the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) becomes manifest in every birth as soon as he is born, and it does not perish in the interim until he sits at the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
What are these four? Namely, that even for the sake of his life, he does not speak a conscious lie.
Even toward those who are merely objects of ridicule,
he dwells with a resolute intention toward all sentient beings, being free from deceit and guile;
and he conceives the perception of a teacher toward all bodhisattvas.
He circulates [the gift] throughout the four directions;
and those beings whom he brings to maturity,
he encourages them all toward unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, without longing for any other vehicle.

Kāśyapa, for a bodhisattva endowed with these four qualities, the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) becomes manifest in every birth as soon as he is born, and he does not lose it in the interim until he sits at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa).
Regarding this, it is said: // 4 //
They do not speak falsehood even for the sake of their lives;
they always utter speech endowed with meaning,
being free from deceit and guile.
With resolute intention, he always regards sentient beings;
those pure beings who have set out for awakening, he considers them to be Teachers. Bodhisattva...
Having established mindfulness toward the Teacher, he proclaims their praise in the four directions;
and he brings those beings who are to be ripened to maturity.
They encourage others toward unsurpassed knowledge;
for those established in these qualities, the mind is never deluded regarding awakening. 3.

KP.5: "Kāśyapa, when a bodhisattva is possessed of four qualities, whatever unwholesome dharmas have arisen are exhausted, and he does not increase [in virtue] by means of those qualities. What are the four? Namely, for one who is conceited, the pursuit of the mantras of the Lokāyatikas."

O Kāśyapa, for a bodhisattva endowed with these four qualities, whatever wholesome dharmas have arisen do not diminish; rather, they increase through those wholesome dharmas. Regarding this, it is said: // 5 //
The conceited one seeks out worldly philosophy among families... and he hates the sons of the Buddha and the bodhisattvas.
They speak disparagement of them on all sides;
they have neither studied nor heard what was taught by the Jina, yet they reject these words spoken by the Victor.
For one endowed with such qualities,
there is no increase in wholesome qualities;
therefore, [the Blessed One said] that bodhisattva...
One should abandon even these four qualities from afar; by practicing them, one remains very far indeed from awakening,
as distant as the sky is from the earth.

Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva endowed with four qualities possesses the nature of non-retrogression and proceeds toward distinction. What are these four? He seeks what is well-heard and not what is ill-heard; that is to say, he seeks the six perfections and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. He is like a dog toward all sentient beings because of his lack of pride. He is content with the acquisition of the Dharma.
He avoids all wrong livelihoods and is content with the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*). Because of this contentment, he does not reproach others.
Nor does he seek out faults or lapses in others;
and regarding those matters where his own intellect does not penetrate, he does not reject them, taking the Tathāgata himself as the witness.
Only the Tathāgata knows this, not I... [the teaching] proceeds according to the various inclinations of beings who possess diverse dispositions.
Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva endowed with these four qualities possesses the nature of non-retrogression for the sake of attaining excellence.
Regarding this, it is said: 6 //
And he is constantly engaged in skillful means regarding the seat of awakening.
And through freedom from pride, he regards all sentient beings as equal to his own mind;
and he is content with gain that is in accordance with the True Dharma.
Pure in livelihood, established in the noble lineages, he does not reproach others for their offenses,
nor does he seek out the faults of those who have stumbled.
Wherever his intellect does not penetrate,
there he realizes the Tathāgata directly;
"I do not know," [he says], "O Victor, you alone know..."
Infinite awakening has been taught by the Sugata;
having understood these four dharmas,
one should never let go of the supreme distinction.
For one who is established in these dharmas,
the enlightenment praised by the Jinas is not difficult to attain.

KP.7. Kāśyapa, there are these four crooked productions of thought that must be avoided by a bodhisattva. What are the four? Namely: doubt, uncertainty, and hesitation regarding all the qualities of a Buddha; pride, intoxication, hypocrisy, anger, and malice toward all sentient beings; envy and stinginess regarding the gains of others; and the utterance of disparagement, infamy, and ill-repute...
These, Kāśyapa, are the four crooked productions of thought that must be avoided by a bodhisattva. Regarding this, it is said: // 7 //
They harbor doubt and indecision regarding the teachings; they cultivate pride and anger toward sentient beings;
and they practice stinginess and envy toward the gains of others.
He who does not bestow favor upon the Victor,
and who always spreads ill-repute, dispraise, and infamy among the Bodhisattvas, is unwise.
A Bodhisattva should always avoid these four crooked states of mind and [adhere to] the side of virtue. 2.

KP.8. Kāśyapa, there are these four upright characteristics of an upright bodhisattva. What are the four? Namely: having fallen into an offense, he does not conceal it but confesses and reveals it; he becomes free from the underlying tendencies (*paryutthāna*). He does not hide that truthful speech by which there might be loss of kingdom, loss of wealth, or even an obstacle to body and life; nor does he speak with words that are evasive or shifting.
In the face of all injuries from others—whether they be insults, revilings, censures, disparagements, beatings, threats, killings, or imprisonments—he considers himself alone at fault.
Taking refuge in the ripening of karma, he does not become angry with others nor harbor resentment.
He becomes firmly established in faith.
Relying on the purity of his intention, he has faith even in those qualities of a Buddha that are entirely beyond belief.
Kāśyapa, these four are the characteristics of rectitude for a bodhisattva who is upright. Regarding this, it is said: // 8 //
Having fallen into an offense, they do not conceal it; they confess and disclose it out of fear of this fault.
They do not [sacrifice] their life for the sake of wealth or sovereignty.
Even when others speak of one with contemptuous notions—
whether through abuse, disparagement, or defamation;
or through acts of killing, binding, or confinement— one should maintain the perception of them as benefactors.
Not being at fault oneself, one does not become angry with others; bearing the burden of one's own karma, one has no resentment.
Such a person has faith in the awakening of the Sugatas.

Established in faith and endowed with purity of intention, these qualities characterized by uprightness have been proclaimed by the Victor; they should be cultivated by the most excellent of beings. 3.

KP.9. Kāśyapa, there are these four types of bodhisattvas who are like mules. What are the four? They are: one who dwells in the Dharma but is arrogant on account of what he has heard, and yet does not practice it; one who dwells in the Dharma but is arrogant on account of the instruction regarding the practice of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, and yet does not desire to listen to his teachers and preceptors.

He squanders what has been given out of faith, and having broken his vow, he consumes that which was given out of faith; and seeing Bodhisattvas who have attained the state of the well-trained noble steed, he is disrespectful and full of pride. Kāśyapa, these four are the unruly mules among Bodhisattvas. Regarding this, it is said: 9.
One who dwells in arrogance because of what they have heard does not proceed according to the instruction;
being arrogant, he pursues all worldly dharmas and never listens to the speech of the Noble Ones. Having abandoned his vow, he constantly consumes the fine foods given out of faith.
Even upon seeing Bodhisattvas who have attained the state of being worthy of honor, he shows them no respect;
that perverse one increases his pride and serves Bodhisattvas with hypocrisy.
These perverse ones were described by the Sugata as "wild colts"; these sons of the Jina should be avoided.

KP.10: "Kāśyapa, there are these four thoroughbred bodhisattvas. What are the four? They are: one who hears what has been well-heard and practices accordingly; one who relies on the meaning and not on the letter; one who is receptive to instruction and admonition;
and one who is easy to speak with and performs deeds well done."
Having emerged from service to the guru, he partakes of the food of the well-bred horse (*ājāneya*).

With unshakable ethical discipline and meditative concentration, having attained the state of a tamed and well-bred one, he becomes respectful and reverent upon seeing bodhisattvas; he inclines toward them, leans toward them, and tends toward them, longing for their virtues. Kāśyapa, these are the four types of well-bred bodhisattvas. On this point, it is said: 10.
Whatever he hears, he makes it well-heard;
established in the practice of the essence of the Dharma and its meaning,
he receives the instruction with reverence.
Easy to speak with, he serves his teacher out of a desire for the Dharma;
always established in ethical conduct and meditative concentration,
he eats excellent food while restrained by virtue.
They are full of reverence and courtesy, inclined toward that [virtue], delighting in it, and longing for its qualities—
those sons of the Jina who have attained the state of the noble-born.
He gazes upon her constantly with love;
these four, O Sugata, are declared by the Sugata to be the sons who have attained the state of a noble steed. 3.
KP.11: Kāśyapa, there are these four lapses of a bodhisattva.
What are the four? Trusting in sentient beings who have not been ripened is a lapse of a bodhisattva;
revealing the sublime Buddha-dharma to sentient beings who have not become fit vessels is a lapse of a bodhisattva; [failing to do so] toward those who possess sublime resolve...

Proclaiming the Hīnayāna to sentient beings is a transgression of a bodhisattva; and showing contempt for those sentient beings who are well-established, virtuous, and possessed of wholesome qualities, while gathering together those who are immoral and of evil character, is a transgression of a bodhisattva. Kāśyapa, these are the four transgressions of a bodhisattva.
In this regard, the following is said: // 10 //
One should not place trust in those who are unripened; one should not speak of the sublime Dharma to those who are not vessels.
That bodhisattva should never reveal the sublime Dharmas to those of the inferior vehicle.
One should not disparage those who are correctly established, endowed with the virtues of ethical conduct, and possessed of wholesome qualities.
Bodhisattvas should not accept those beings who are immoral, and they should avoid unwholesome qualities.
Knowing these four transgressions, bodhisattvas should shun them from afar;
for by practicing these, one does not awaken to enlightenment. Therefore, the wise should avoid these things. 3.

KP.12: Kāśyapa, there are these four paths of a bodhisattva. What are the four? Equanimity of mind toward all sentient beings; causing all sentient beings to undertake the wisdom of a Buddha; teaching the Dharma equally to all sentient beings; and right application toward all sentient beings.
These, Kāśyapa, are the four paths of a bodhisattva. Regarding this, it is said: 12.
One should always maintain an even mind toward all beings and, with the wisdom of a Buddha, encourage them here in the Buddha-vehicle.
One should teach the Dharma praised by the Jinas with a mind full of faith toward all beings.
Rightly applied and firmly established in practice, one should conduct oneself with equanimity toward all beings.
The sons of the Conquerors always cultivate these four paths praised by the Conquerors. // 3 //
KP.13: Kāśyapa, there are these four bad friends and unwholesome companions of a bodhisattva who should be avoided by a bodhisattva.
What are the four?
A monk belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas who is engaged in his own welfare; and one belonging to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas who has little purpose and little activity.

The materialist who possesses diverse spells and eloquence; and whichever person one serves from whom there is a gathering of worldly gain and not a gathering of the Dharma—Kāśyapa, these four are a bodhisattva’s bad friends and unwholesome companions, and they should be avoided by a bodhisattva. In this regard, it is said:
Those disciples who are devoted to their own welfare and practice the yoga of those who have gone forth;
and also the Pratyekabuddhas who have few duties, avoid contact with trivial matters; and those fools who abandon Lokāyata, wherein discourse is taught for the sake of disputation.
Those whom one serves would result in the acquisition of material things, but not the acquisition of the Dharma;

having abandoned those four [types of persons], Bodhisattvas rely upon four types of spiritual friends. These bad friends, joined with unwholesome companions, should be avoided from afar by the Victor.
KP.14 Kāśyapa, there are these four true spiritual friends of a bodhisattva.
What are the four?

A petitioner is a true spiritual friend of a bodhisattva, as they serve to support the path to enlightenment; a Dharma-preacher is a true spiritual friend of a bodhisattva, as they serve to support learning and wisdom.
One who encourages others to go forth into homelessness is a true spiritual friend for a bodhisattva, serving to support all roots of virtue.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, serve as the true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) for a bodhisattva, leading to the support of all the qualities of a Buddha.
These, Kāśyapa, are the true spiritual friends of a bodhisattva; regarding this, it is said: // 12 //
He is a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) to donors, being a recipient for the sake of embracing awakening (*bodhi*).
One who speaks of the meaning of the Dharma and produces learning and wisdom is declared by the Sugata to be a spiritual friend.
Furthermore, those who, having gone forth, encourage others to do the same are said by the Sugata to be the root of friendship.
The Buddha is the friend of the sons of the Sugata for the sake of supporting the path of the Perfectly Awakened One.
Indeed, these four are praised by the Jinas as the spiritual friends of the sons of the Sugata. By constantly attending to these without negligence, one attains the awakening taught by the Sugata. 3.

KP.15. Kāśyapa, there are these four who are counterfeits of a bodhisattva. What are the four? He seeks gain and honor, not the Dharma; he seeks fame, renown, and praise, not virtuous qualities; he seeks his own happiness, not the removal of the suffering of sentient beings; and he seeks the excellence of a retinue.
Kāśyapa, these four are counterfeit bodhisattvas who do not seek seclusion; regarding this, it is said: // 14 //

He seeks gain, not the Dharma; he seeks fame, not these very virtues; he does not seek to remove the suffering of sentient beings, but seeks constant happiness for himself; he desires the qualities of a retinue, not solitude; he is attached to pleasure, not attached to virtues.
These four are described as counterfeits that should be avoided by bodhisattvas.
KP.16: "Kāśyapa, these four are the true qualities of a bodhisattva.
What are the four? He has resolute conviction in emptiness, yet he has deep faith in the ripening of karma."

He accepts selflessness and possesses great compassion toward all sentient beings; his intention is directed toward nirvāṇa while his application is directed toward saṃsāra; he practices giving for the sake of maturing sentient beings and does not expect a karmic reward.
Kāśyapa, these four qualities are the genuine qualities of a bodhisattva. Regarding this, it is said: // 15 //
He always has faith in phenomena as empty and believes in the ripening of karma;

established in the equanimity of selflessness through patience, he constantly generates compassion for sentient beings. His existence is ever directed toward nirvāṇa, yet his application remains within saṃsāra.
And for the sake of bringing others to maturity, he gives gifts, yet he does not long for the karmic fruition of his actions.
KP.17: Kāśyapa, there are these four great acquisitions for a bodhisattva. Which four?
Encountering the arising of a Buddha;
hearing the six perfections; and seeing a Dharma-preacher with an unobstructed mind.
“Kāśyapa, for one who is heedful and delights in dwelling in the forest, these are the four great acquisitions of a bodhisattva.
Regarding this, it is said: // 16 //
In all births, he pleases the Buddhas and hears the six perfections;
with a serene mind, he always beholds the Dharma-preachers with reverence. Always heedful, he dwells in the forest, and therein he always finds delight.
Four dharmas have been proclaimed by the Sugata as great treasures for the sons of the Conqueror. //2//

KP.18: Kāśyapa, there are these four qualities by which a bodhisattva transcends the path of Māra. What are the four? Not abandoning the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), having a mind free from hostility toward all sentient beings, the thorough understanding of all views that have been formed, and not holding any sentient being in contempt. These, Kāśyapa, are the four qualities by which a bodhisattva transcends the path of Māra.
In this regard, the following is said: // 17 //
They do not abandon the mind set on enlightenment, they constantly relinquish resentment toward sentient beings,
they cast off all positions of false views, and they do not hold themselves in high esteem above the body of sentient beings—
these four qualities have been taught by the Sugata for the purpose of transcending Māra.
Having practiced this, they become Jinas, the Aṅgīrasas, the peerless Leaders.
KP.19: Kāśyapa, these four qualities lead to the gathering of all wholesome dharmas for a bodhisattva.
What are the four? Delight in dwelling in the forest without guile;
the means of attraction (*saṅgrahavastu*) toward all sentient beings without seeking recompense; the sacrifice of body and life; and insatiability in the pursuit of the sublime Dharma.
Kāśyapa, these four qualities lead a bodhisattva to the accumulation of all roots of virtue and to the gathering of all wholesome dharmas. Regarding this, it is said: // 18 //
Dwelling in the forest, free from hypocrisy, gathering in beings according to what was taught by the Jina;
renouncing both body and life, he undertook the search for the True Dharma.
And he was always insatiable in the accumulation of manifold roots of virtue.
And for the sake of gathering wholesome qualities, four dharmas were taught by the Sugata. 2.

KP.20: "Kāśyapa, these four are the immeasurable accumulations of merit for a bodhisattva. What are the four? Giving the Dharma with a mind free from worldly desire; great compassion toward beings who are immoral; proclaiming the thought of awakening to all beings; and serving those beings who are weak with patience."
Kāśyapa, these four are the immeasurable accumulations of merit for a bodhisattva; regarding this, it is said: // 19 //
The gift of the Dharma praised by the Victors,
with a mind that is pure, free from worldly motives,
and devoid of [attachment to] conduct, as well as intense compassion.
One generates the mind for enlightenment in others;
one practices patience toward those who are weak; and the inclusion within the teachings is also spoken of.
Having cultivated these, they become Victors;
therefore, these four groups of eight Bodhisattva qualities should always be practiced. Abandon the [remaining] eight.
Those who create obstacles to enlightenment,
as well as others— having served twelve wise ones— he attains enlightenment, touching the nectar of immortality.
And those supreme beings who uphold, recite, and proclaim this guidance of the Dharma— the Jina declares their merit to be infinite.
Those who describe the immeasurable qualities of the Victorious One,
and those who, having filled with jewels as many millions of fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, should give them away—
Or whoever should recite even a single four-line verse from this [text], the merit of that cannot be calculated. //5//
KP.21. “Kāśyapa, these four qualities lead a bodhisattva to transcend the afflictions associated with ignorance.

What are the four? They are: restraint in ethical discipline, upholding the true Dharma, and giving lamps, even to those who are merely acquaintances. Kāśyapa, these four qualities lead a bodhisattva to transcend the afflictions associated with ignorance.”
KP.22: Kāśyapa, these four qualities lead a bodhisattva to unobstructed knowledge.
What are the four? Namely: restraint of the sense faculties; explaining the profound meaning; not disparaging others because of one's own gains; and being without envy regarding the gains of others.
Kāśyapa, these four qualities lead a bodhisattva to unobstructed knowledge. // 22 //

“Kāśyapa, one is certainly not called a ‘bodhisattva mahāsattva’ by name alone. Rather, Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with the practice of the Dharma, the practice of equanimity, the practice of the wholesome, and the practice of truthfulness is called a ‘bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva who is endowed with thirty-two qualities is called a ‘bodhisattva.’”
What are the thirty-two? Namely: (1) the resolute intention for the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings;
(2) the introduction of others to the knowledge of omniscience; (3) not disparaging the knowledge of others by thinking "I am one who follows the path," through the absence of pride;
and (4) firmness of resolute intention.
Through the state of unfeigned affection; through being an ultimate friend;
and through having a mind of equanimity toward both friends and enemies.
KP.24 Until the very limit of nirvāṇa: speaking no falsehoods; addressing others with a smiling face; not taking up burdens that have not been undertaken;

possessing great compassion toward all sentient beings without limitation; having a mind free from weariness; and being insatiable in hearing and understanding the meaning of the true Dharma, beginning with the quest for it.
By seeing faults in one's own transgressions; by not being angry at the transgressions of others and instead urging them toward the recognition of their faults;
and by cultivating the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) in all wrong paths.
Generosity that does not expect a karmic maturation; ethical discipline that is independent of rebirth in any state of existence; patience that is unimpeded toward all sentient beings;
and vigor for the undertaking of all roots of virtue. (KP.25)
The meditative absorptions cultivated through the formless [realms];
wisdom embraced by skillful means;
and skillful means associated with the four bases of sympathy.
Friendliness toward those who possess virtue and those who lack it; listening to the Dharma with reverence;
dwelling in the forest with reverence; lack of delight in the various diversions of the world; and freedom from false views.
Longing for the Hīnayāna;
failing to perceive the benefits of the Mahāyāna;
avoiding evil friends; and attending upon virtuous friends.
The accomplishment of the four divine abodes;
sporting with the five supernormal powers;
and relying upon gnosis.
Not abandoning sentient beings who abide in either right practice or wrong practice; speaking with a single voice;
holding truth in high esteem;
and being insatiable in the full realization of the roots of virtue.
“Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with these thirty-two qualities is called a ‘bodhisattva mahāsattva,’ because he is preceded by the thought of awakening (bodhicitta).”
In this regard, the following is said:

Resolving with a resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) for the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings in order to transcend toward the knowledge of the Omniscient One, one asks: "Am I worthy or unworthy?
This refers to the absence of self-reproach, the absence of pride regarding knowledge, firmness of intention, and unfeigned affection.
2. Toward sentient beings, there is extreme and constant friendliness until they reach final liberation;

toward friend and foe, there is equanimity of mind, a smiling countenance, and speech that is truthful. 3. Regarding the burden that has been taken up... [there is] steadfastness and likewise compassion for sentient beings.
KP.27 There is no weariness in the quest for the true Dharma; one is insatiable regarding what has been heard; one does not dwell on the fault of a lapse;
and even when another is angry, one should not be provoked to anger.
The pliancy of the mind in the modes of conduct (īryāpatha),
the relinquishing [of self-interest], and the lack of expectation for karmic fruition—
this is the arising of ethical discipline within the realms of existence.
Patience toward sentient beings, free from resentment;
vigor for the accumulation of the wholesome;
and the most excellent meditative absorption of the formless realm.
Wisdom is embraced by skillful means, and skillful means is embraced by the four means of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*);
[this applies] to those of immoral conduct and those of moral conduct, and through both types of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
One should listen to the Dharma with reverence at the proper time, and dwell with reverence in the peace of the forest.
One should not take delight in the various worldly realms, nor should one take delight in inferior vehicles;
rather, one should conceive a longing for the sublime vehicles and avoid sinful friends.
One should always attend upon spiritual friends and cultivate the four sublime abodes (brahmavihāras).
One should always sport with the five superknowledges (abhijñās) and follow after wisdom.
One should never abandon those endowed with correct practice, nor ever any others for a second time. 8–9 KP.28–29.
One should always be an advocate of the single path and always possess reverence for the truth;

one should cultivate the qualities praised by the Jinas, having made the mind of awakening the foremost. These thirty-two qualities have been proclaimed by the Sugata as the practices to be cultivated by one who delights in the Sugata’s teaching.
Those Bodhisattvas who are endowed with these qualities have been proclaimed by the Sugata. 11.
“Kāśyapa, I shall teach you the instructions through the presentation of similes,

by which instructions for the presentation of similes a bodhisattva mahāsattva makes known the qualities [of a bodhisattva]. For example, Kāśyapa, just as this great earth is the sustenance for all beings, remaining unchanging and without expectation of recompense, even so, Kāśyapa, from the first production of the thought of awakening until sitting at the seat of awakening, a bodhisattva is the sustenance for all beings, remaining unchanging and without expectation of recompense.”
In this regard, the following is said:
Just as the earth, which sustains all living beings, remains free from change and does not expect any recompense,

so too the Bodhisattva established in the first mind remains free from change and does not expect any recompense until he becomes a Buddha, the supreme Victor; for he is unsurpassed and sustains all living beings.
Regarding both son and enemy as equal, he constantly seeks the supreme, foremost enlightenment.

KP.30 Just as, Kāśyapa, the water element causes all grasses, shrubs, herbs, and trees to grow, even so, Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva whose intention is pure, dwelling while pervading all sentient beings with loving-kindness, causes all the white dharmas of all sentient beings to grow.
Regarding this, it is said:
Just as the water element causes grasses, shrubs, medicinal herbs, trees, and the various kinds of medicinal plants and grains to grow,
even so the bodhisattva of pure intention radiates loving-kindness toward sentient beings infinitely; having radiated it, he gradually [teaches] various dharmas.
Increasing in pure qualities,
he attains the awakening of the Victors,
having struck down Māra along with his power and his army.

KP.31 Just as, Kāśyapa, the element of fire brings all crops to maturity, even so, Kāśyapa, the wisdom of a bodhisattva brings to maturity all the pure dharmas of all sentient beings. Regarding this, it is said: 3.
Just as fire ripens all crops, grasses, and medicinal herbs,
even so does the wisdom of the sons of the Sugata cause the virtuous qualities of people to increase.

KP.32 Just as, Kāśyapa, the wind element establishes all Buddha-fields, even so, Kāśyapa, the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of a bodhisattva establishes all the qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadharma*). Regarding this, it is said:
Just as the wind establishes various fields according to the diverse intentions of the Buddhas...
For it is through skillful means that the sons of the Conquerors thus establish the supreme teachings spoken by the Sugata.
KP.33 Just as, Kāśyapa, the fourfold army of Māra the Evil One cannot be overcome or defeated by all the gods,
even so, Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva of pure intention cannot be overcome or defeated by any Māras.
KP.34 Just as, Kāśyapa, during the bright fortnight the lunar disc becomes full and increases.
In the same way, Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva whose intention is pure increases in all white dharmas. Regarding this, it is said: "Just as the lunar disk [waxes] during the bright fortnight..."
It is filled, it increases, and it does not diminish;
in just this way, the bodhisattva of pure intention always increases through pure qualities.

KP.35 Just as, Kāśyapa, the orb of the sun brings illumination to sentient beings by means of its rays emitted all at once, even so, Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva brings the illumination of wisdom to sentient beings by means of the rays of insight emitted all at once. Regarding this, it is said: 7
Just as the sun, by means of its rays emitted all at once, causes beings to shine,
so too does the Son of the Jinas [illuminate] with the rays of his wisdom.
Through wisdom, one brings illumination to sentient beings.

KP.36 Just as, Kāśyapa, wherever the lion, the king of beasts, goes forth, he goes forth everywhere entirely without fear; even so, Kāśyapa, wherever a bodhisattva established in the qualities of ethical discipline, learning, and virtue goes forth, he goes forth everywhere entirely without fear or terror.
In this regard, it is said: Just as the lion, the king of beasts, the maned one, goes wherever he wishes without fear,
even so the bodhisattva, well-established in ethical discipline, learning, and knowledge, goes wherever he wishes.
KP.37 Just as, Kāśyapa, a well-tamed elephant-nāga does not grow weary from carrying all burdens,
even so, Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva whose mind is well-tamed does not grow weary from carrying all the burdens of all sentient beings. On this point, it is said:
Just as a powerful, well-trained ox carrying a load does not succumb to weariness,
so too a Bodhisattva with a well-tamed mind does not experience fatigue from the burden of sentient beings.
KP.38 Just as, Kāśyapa, a lotus born in water is not defiled by the water, even so, Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva born in the world is not defiled by worldly dharmas. Regarding this, it is said: 10.
Just as the red lotus, born in the water, is not defiled by water or by mud,
so too the Bodhisattva, though born in the world, is never defiled by worldly dharmas.

KP.39 Just as, Kāśyapa, a tree whose branches have been cut off grows forth once again if its root is not destroyed, even so, Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva whose afflictions have been severed by skillful means grows forth once again within the triple world if his connection with all roots of merit is not destroyed. Regarding this, it is said: 11.
Just as a tree cut from its branches grows back again if the root is firm and unharmed,
so too one who is struck down by skillful means grows back if the fetters at the root have been thoroughly abandoned.

Kāśyapa, it is just as, for example, when the masses of water from the great rivers in the various cardinal and intermediate directions enter the great ocean, they all become of one single taste, namely, the taste of salt; even so, Kāśyapa, the roots of virtue accumulated through various means by a bodhisattva, when dedicated toward awakening, all become of one single taste, which is the taste of liberation.
Regarding this, it is said:

Just as the water of various rivers, once entered into the great ocean, becomes of one single taste, so too the wholesome roots accumulated through various means, when dedicated, become of one single taste in awakening. //12//

KP.41 Just as, Kāśyapa, the gods of the Four Great Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa gods are established upon Mount Sumeru, even so, Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva’s omniscience is established upon the roots of non-virtue of the thought of awakening. Regarding this, it is said:
Just as the hosts of gods of the Four Great Kings and the Trāyastriṃśas are established on Sumeru.
In the same way, Bodhisattvas established in virtue, having attained omniscience, preach the Dharma.

KP.42 Just as, Kāśyapa, kings supported by their ministers carry out all royal affairs, even so, Kāśyapa, the wisdom of a bodhisattva supported by skillful means carries out all the works of a Buddha. Regarding this, it is said: 14.

Just as a king, through the gathering of his ministers, constantly accomplishes all his tasks, so too does the Bodhisattva, through the gathering of skillful means, constantly accomplish the purpose of the Buddhas by means of wisdom.

KP.43 Just as, Kāśyapa, when the sky is cloudless and free from mist, there is no source for rain, even so, Kāśyapa, from a Bodhisattva who has heard little, there is no noble gateway for the rain of the True Dharma. Regarding this, it is said: Just as in a cloudless sky, free from mist, The source of rain is never found.
Furthermore, the teaching of the Dharma is never obtained by a bodhisattva from one who has heard little.

KP.44 Just as, Kāśyapa, streams of rain arising from dense clouds pour down upon the crops, even so, Kāśyapa, the rain of the True Dharma of a Bodhisattva, arising from the cloud of Great Compassion, pours down upon sentient beings. Regarding this, it is said: 16
Just as a vast cloud accompanied by lightning brings satisfaction through its continuous rain,
so too does the stream of rain arising from the cloud of the True Dharma.
In the same way, the bodhisattva satisfies sentient beings.

KP.45 Just as, Kāśyapa, wherever a universal monarch (cakravartin) is born, there the seven precious jewels are born; even so, Kāśyapa, wherever a bodhisattva is born, there the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) are born. Regarding this, it is said: 17.
For wherever a wheel-turning monarch is born, there his seven jewels appear;
and wherever a bodhisattva is born, there his seven factors of awakening appear.
KP.46 Just as, Kāśyapa, wherever there is a source for the entry of a precious gem, there is a source for the entry of many hundreds of thousands of kārṣāpaṇas;
even so, Kāśyapa, wherever there is a source for the entry of a bodhisattva,
there is a source for the entry of many hundreds of thousands of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
In this regard, it is said: 18.
Just as when a precious jewel exists, there come to be many *karṣāpaṇa* coins... there they come to be.
And wherever there is an influx of the mind of enlightenment, there is also a great influx of śrāvakas.

KP.47 Just as, Kāśyapa, the enjoyments and possessions of the Trāyastriṃśa gods dwelling in the Miśrakāvana grove remain equal, even so, Kāśyapa, for a bodhisattva whose intention is pure, there is right application toward all sentient beings. Regarding this, it is said: 19
Just as the activities of the gods, when they have come together, remain intermingled among those who stand there,
even so the bodhisattva of pure intention applies himself correctly toward sentient beings.
KP.48: Kāśyapa, it is just as poison, when held under the influence of mantras and medicinal herbs, does not cause death;
even so, Kāśyapa, the poison of a bodhisattva’s afflictions, being held under the influence of wisdom and skillful means, is unable to cause a downfall.
Regarding this, it is said: 20.
Just as poison, through the application of a mantra, is rendered incapable of harming people by its action, so too a wise Bodhisattva here cannot be cast down by the afflictions.

KP.49 Just as, Kāśyapa, whatever heap of refuse there may be in great cities becomes beneficial in sugar-cane fields, rice fields, and vineyards, even so, Kāśyapa, whatever affliction belongs to a bodhisattva becomes beneficial for omniscience. Regarding this, it is said: 21.
Just as refuse in cities is beneficial in sugar-cane fields for making them clean,
even so do the afflictions provide benefit to a bodhisattva regarding the Dharma of the Victors.

KP.50 Just as, Kāśyapa, one who has not been trained in archery [is incapable of] grasping a weapon, even so, Kāśyapa, should the knowledge of a Bodhisattva who has heard little regarding the skill in the investigation of phenomena, the examination of meanings, and the grasping of the meaning be viewed. 22.

KP.51 Just as, Kāśyapa, a potter applies a great fire to his crude vessels, even so, Kāśyapa, should it be understood that a Bodhisattva’s teaching of the sublime Dharma to those of immature wisdom is like this.

KP.52 Therefore, Kāśyapa, a Bodhisattva who wishes to train in this Dharma discourse of the Great Jewel Heap (Mahāratnakūṭa) must apply themselves to the Dharma with fundamental rationality (*yoniśas*).
In this regard, Kāśyapa, what is the application of the Dharma with fundamental rationality? It is the authentic discernment of all phenomena.

And what, Kāśyapa, is the authentic discernment of all phenomena? That in which, Kāśyapa, there is no discernment of a self, no discernment of a sentient being, no living being, no nourished being, no person, no human, and no man— this, Kāśyapa, is called the middle way, the authentic discernment of phenomena.

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, the middle way, which is the correct analytical observation of phenomena, is that which is neither the observation that form is permanent nor the observation that it is impermanent; and that which is neither the observation that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are permanent nor the observation that they are impermanent— this, Kāśyapa, is called the middle way, the correct analytical observation of phenomena.

KP.54 That which is the contemplation that the earth element is neither permanent nor impermanent; that which is the contemplation that the water element, the fire element, or the wind element is neither permanent nor impermanent;

that which is the contemplation that the space element and the consciousness element are neither permanent nor impermanent—this, Kāśyapa, is called the middle way, the true contemplation of phenomena.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, the middle way is the correct analytical observation of phenomena (*dharmāṇāṃ bhūtapratyavekṣā*).
That which is the analytical observation that the sense-base of the eye is neither permanent nor impermanent—this, Kāśyapa, is called the middle way, the correct analytical observation of phenomena.
This applies likewise up to the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, which are neither permanent nor impermanent.
This, Kāśyapa, is called the middle way, the true contemplation of phenomena.

"Permanent," Kāśyapa, is one extreme; "impermanent," Kāśyapa, is the second extreme. That which is the middle between these two—permanence and impermanence—is formless, invisible, non-manifest, non-communicative, baseless, and homeless.

This, Kāśyapa, is called the middle way, the true discernment of phenomena. "Self," Kāśyapa, is one extreme; "selflessness" is the second extreme. That which is the middle between self and selflessness—formless, invisible, non-manifest, non-communicative, non-abiding, and homeless—this, Kāśyapa, is called [the middle way].
The middle way is the correct discernment of phenomena.
Kāśyapa, "real mind" is one extreme; Kāśyapa, "unreal mind" is the second extreme.
Kāśyapa, that which is without volition, without mind, and without consciousness—this, Kāśyapa, is called the middle way.
The correct analytical observation of phenomena (dharmāṇāṃ bhūtapratyavekṣā) is as follows:

Kāśyapa, to say that all phenomena—whether wholesome or unwholesome, mundane or supramundane, faulty or faultless, with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned—are "defilement" is one extreme; Kāśyapa, to say they are "purification" is [the other extreme].
The second extreme is that which follows after these two extremes, their expression, and their verbalization;
this, Kāśyapa, is called the middle way, the true discernment of phenomena.

"It exists," Kāśyapa, is one extreme; "it does not exist" is the second extreme. That which is the middle between these two extremes, Kāśyapa, is called the middle way, the true discernment of phenomena.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, that which I have declared to you is this:

namely, conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces; conditioned by the formative forces is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness are name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases is contact; conditioned by contact is sensation; and conditioned by sensation is craving.

With craving as condition, grasping arises; with grasping as condition, becoming arises; with becoming as condition, birth arises; with birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.
With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases.
From the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense-bases cease...
[this], Kāśyapa, is called the middle way, the true discernment of phenomena.

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, the authentic discernment of phenomena is this: it is not that one makes phenomena empty by means of emptiness, for phenomena themselves are empty; it is not that one makes phenomena signless by means of the signless, for phenomena themselves are signless; it is not that one makes phenomena wishless by means of the wishless, for phenomena themselves are wishless; it is not that one constructs phenomena by means of non-constructing.

Since phenomena are indeed unconditioned, one does not by way of non-arising make phenomena non-arisen; and since phenomena are indeed unarisen, one does not by way of non-birth make phenomena unborn; and since phenomena are indeed ungraspable, one does not by way of non-grasping make phenomena ungraspable; for phenomena are indeed ungraspable.
In this way, one makes untainted phenomena untainted, and the phenomena themselves are indeed untainted.
Likewise, that which makes phenomena lack intrinsic nature by means of not having intrinsic nature, and the phenomena themselves are indeed without intrinsic nature;

likewise, that which is the absence of intrinsic nature in phenomena by virtue of not having intrinsic nature—that which does not perceive any intrinsic nature—this kind of discernment, Kāśyapa, is called the middle way regarding phenomena.
The discernment of reality.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, emptiness is certainly not for the sake of destroying the existence of a person; the person itself is emptiness, emptiness itself is emptiness,
it is absolute emptiness,
and it is the emptiness of the past limit.
The emptiness of the future and the emptiness of the present—
Kāśyapa, rely upon emptiness, do not rely upon the person.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, those who rely upon emptiness by means of apprehending emptiness [are mistaken].

“Kāśyapa, I say that they are lost and utterly destroyed from this teaching. Indeed, Kāśyapa, it is better to rely on a person-view as large as Mount Sumeru than to have the defiled view of emptiness belonging to one who is conceited.
Why is that? Because for those who have fallen into a person-view, Kāśyapa, emptiness is the escape; but by what, Kāśyapa, will those with a view of emptiness themselves escape?”

KP.65. "Kāśyapa, it is just as if some man were to fall ill, and a physician were to give him medicine; yet that medicine, having expelled all the humors, remained in his stomach and did not come out. What do you think, Kāśyapa? Would that sick man be freed from that illness?"
"If that medicine, having expelled the humors located in all parts of the body,
were not itself to exit from the stomach," the Blessed One said,
"the illness of that person would become even more severe."

"If that medicine, having expelled all the humors, should not itself come out along with them from the stomach," the Blessed One said, "In the very same way, Kāśyapa, emptiness is the escape from all views. However, Kāśyapa, one who holds a view of emptiness, I declare to be incurable."
In this regard, the following is said:
Just as a physician might give a purgative to a person to suppress a disease, yet the humors are stirred up but do not exit, and consequently neither the cause nor the affliction is pacified;
even so, for those who have fallen into the thicket of views, emptiness is indeed the supreme escape.
She quickly...
KP.70... those who [realize] emptiness as well.
It is just as if, Kāśyapa, an oil lamp does not think, "I am dispelling the darkness.
Nevertheless, when the oil lamp is lit, darkness departs in dependence upon the light.
And that which is the oil lamp, Kāśyapa, and that which is the darkness—both of these are empty.
Ungraspable, empty, and inactive—just so, Kāśyapa, both knowledge and ignorance, as well as non-ignorance, these two are both empty, ungraspable, empty, and inactive. 7.
KP.71. It is just as if, Kāśyapa, in a house, a cave, or a chamber, after the passing of a thousand years, no oil lamp had ever been lit at all;
yet then, some man were to light an oil lamp there.

"What do you think, Kāśyapa? Would that mass of darkness say, 'I have accumulated for a thousand years; I will not depart from here'? He replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One. That mass of darkness has no power to remain once an oil lamp has been lit; it must inevitably depart. The Blessed One said, "In the same way, Kāśyapa, [even] that which has accumulated for hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of eons..."
Even so, Karmic affliction is dispelled by a single instance of wise attention and discerning wisdom.
"The oil lamp," Kāśyapa, is a designation for the noble one's faculty of wisdom;
"the darkness of gloom," Kāśyapa, is a designation for karmic affliction.
In this regard, it is said:
Just as if a lamp were placed in a dwelling by some person after a long time has passed...
[he] would lift it up.
"Behold the disciple endowed with the wholesome, possessed of conditioned virtue.
Kāśyapa, it is just as, for example, the space-element within a mustard seed eaten by woodworms; in the same way, Kāśyapa, the conditioned knowledge of a disciple is to be regarded."
In this regard, it is said:
"Just as the space within a mustard seed that has been eaten by a woodworm is extremely small and limited,
so you should understand that the conditioned knowledge of a śrāvaka is slight and restricted."
KP.79 Just as, Kāśyapa, the element of space exists throughout the ten directions, so should the conditioned knowledge of a bodhisattva be regarded. Regarding this, it is said:
Just as space remains unobstructed throughout all the worlds in the ten directions, so too is the wisdom of the Bodhisattva.
Behold the wisdom produced by the Bodhisattva, which is likewise the foremost in all the world.

KP.80: "Kāśyapa, it is just as if the chief queen of a consecrated Kṣatriya king were to have sexual relations with a poor man, and from that union a son were born. What do you think, Kāśyapa, should he be called a prince? He replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One. The Blessed One said:

In the same way, Kāśyapa, although my disciples are born from the realm of Dharma (dharmadhātu), they nevertheless cannot be called the Tathāgata’s sons who are worthy of consecration. Regarding this, it is said: Just as if a king’s beloved queen were to live together with a poor man, and a son were born to her by him; though he is a prince, he will not become a king.

In the same way, those disciples who are free from passion are never to be consecrated as my sons; for they are devoted solely to their own benefit, whereas the sons of the Buddha are dedicated to the welfare of both themselves and others.
KP.81: "Kāśyapa, it is just as if a consecrated Kṣatriya king were to have intercourse with a lowly maidservant, and from her a son were born to him.
Although, Kāśyapa, he was born from the side of a lowly maidservant, nevertheless, he is still a prince."

Thus it should be said: "In the same way, Kāśyapa, although a bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of awakening may lack the power to discipline sentient beings while wandering in saṃsāra, he must nevertheless be called a son of the Tathāgata. On this point, it is said:
Just as a universal monarch, having entered into union with the queen, might beget a son;
Even though he is born from a slave girl and is called "Prince" by the world,
the Bodhisattva, wandering through the three realms with diminished power in his first thought-moment,
is called a "Son of the Conqueror" and a "Pure Being" because he disciplines sentient beings through generosity and skillful means. 3.
Kāśyapa, it is just as if a universal monarch (cakravartin) were to have a thousand sons, yet none among them were endowed with the marks of a universal monarch; in that case,
the universal monarch would not regard them as his sons.

In the same way, Kāśyapa, even if the Tathāgata is surrounded by a retinue of hundreds of thousands of millions of śrāvakas, and there is not a single bodhisattva among them, the Tathāgata does not conceive the notion that they are his sons. Regarding this, it is said: Just as if a king had a thousand sons, yet not even one son possessed the [auspicious] marks, [he would have no affection for them].
The Best of Men has no such notion regarding them, because they are not capable of bearing that burden;
for indeed, the Buddha would have passed into nirvāṇa with many millions remaining, yet among them there is not a single bodhisattva.
The Sugata has no notion of "son" toward them, since there is no one among them who is a bodhisattva.

Kāśyapa, it is just as if, for example, a prince endowed with the marks of a universal monarch (cakravartin) were conceived in the womb of the chief queen of a wheel-turning king after seven nights; even while he remains in the womb, his faculties unripened and existing in the state of the *kalala* embryo, the gods there conceive an even stronger longing for him.

But it is not so with those princes who have attained strength, swiftness, speed, and power; for what reason? Because he will stand for the non-interruption of the lineage of the wheel-turning monarchs.

In the very same way, Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of awakening, though his faculties are unripened and he is like an embryo in the state of the great elements, is nevertheless far more powerful; therefore, the gods who have seen him before conceive a longing for him.
But it is certainly not so for Arhats who dwell in the eight liberations.
For what reason? Because he will remain for the sake of ensuring that the lineage of the Buddhas is not interrupted.
Regarding this, it is said: 19.

Just as the chief queen of a universal monarch conceives a being endowed with the merits of the marks [of a great man], so too do the powerful gods feel longing for the Bodhisattva who dwells in the womb of the Mother of the Victor; they do not long for princes who have attained worldly power,
but for the Bodhisattva established in one-pointed mind, remaining within saṃsāra while striving for awakening.
The gods and nāgas conceive a longing for him, not for the śrāvakas who meditate on the three liberations.

Kāśyapa, it is just as, for example, a young karaviṅka bird, while still within the shell of its egg and before its eyes have even emerged, surpasses the entire flock of birds by means of its deep, sweet, and resonant cry. In the very same way, Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of awakening, though still enclosed within the shell of ignorance and whose vision is veiled by the cataracts of the darkness and gloom of karma and afflictions, [surpasses] all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas...
He surpasses them, namely, by means of the sound and proclamation resulting from the application and accomplishment of the dedication of roots of virtue. 20.

Just as, Kāśyapa, all the foremost merchants, townspeople, and countryfolk, as well as the vassal kings, pay homage to the prince born at that very moment from the chief queen of a universal monarch (cakravartin), even so, Kāśyapa, the world with its gods pays homage to a bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of awakening. 21.
Kāśyapa, it is just as if a single *vaiḍūrya* jewel, even if only the size of Mount Sumeru, would outshine a heap of glass beads;
in the very same way, Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva who has first generated the mind of awakening outshines all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Regarding this, it is said: 22.
Just as a radiant lapis lazuli gem outshines a multitude of glass gems,
even so does a bodhisattva in their first thought-moment surpass the qualities of the individual śrāvakas.
KP.86 Just as, Kāśyapa, all the foremost merchants, townspeople, and countryfolk, as well as the vassal kings, pay homage to the prince born at that very moment from the chief queen of a king;
even so, Kāśyapa, the world together with its gods pays homage to a bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of awakening. Regarding this, it is said: 23.

Just as when a son is born to a king, a lord of the earth, whose limbs are adorned with the marks [of a great man], the subordinate kings and the citizens bow down upon seeing that prince as soon as he is born; even so, as soon as the Bodhisattva was born, they bowed to that son of the Conqueror-King who possessed the excellent marks.
Even the gods of the world pay homage to one whose mind is serene and who is filled with great respect.

KP.87. Kāśyapa, it is just as, for example, whatever medicinal herbs grow on the Himavat, the king of mountains, are all without "mine-ness," without possession, and free from conceptual construction;
and wherever diseases arise, they pacify those very diseases.

In the same way, Kāśyapa, whatever medicine of wisdom a bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of awakening gathers, he gathers it all without conceptual construction, with a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
The medical treatment proceeds; regarding this, it is said: 24.
Those medicines that grow on Himavat, the king of mountains, are free from conceit and free from conceptual construction.
Wherever they are brought, some Sons of the Victor pacify that sickness and remove old age; others gather the medicine of wisdom, having abandoned conceptual construction.
For the sake of the welfare of all, they gather everything while practicing healing with an impartial mind toward sentient beings.

KP.88 Just as, Kāśyapa, the new moon is venerated, whereas the full moon is not venerated in that same way, even so, Kāśyapa, those who have faith in me should venerate the Bodhisattva who is more powerful, and not the Tathāgata. Why is that? Because the Tathāgatas are born from the Bodhisattvas. On this point, it is said: 25
Everyone pays homage to the new moon, but they do not pay homage to it when it is full;
likewise, the son of the Conqueror who has faith should bow to the Bodhisattva, but not to the Conquerors.
Kāśyapa, it is just as, for example, a matrix is the precursor to the knowledge that grasps all treatises;
in the very same way, Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of awakening is the precursor to the unsurpassed empowerment of all the Buddha’s miraculous transformations.

KP.90. Just as, Kāśyapa, no one has ever previously paid homage to the form of a star while abandoning the lunar disk, even so, Kāśyapa, a wise person who has undertaken my training never pays homage to a śrāvaka while neglecting a bodhisattva. Regarding this, it is said: 26.
O Moon, never have the hosts of stars been honored by anyone while bypassing you;
likewise, a disciple who has undertaken the training should never abandon my own son and pay homage [to another].
KP.91 Just as, Kāśyapa, even if the world with its gods were to polish a glass trinket, that glass trinket could never become a precious *vaiḍūrya* gem;

in the same way, Kāśyapa, even if a *śrāvaka* is endowed with all the trainings in ethical discipline, the ascetic qualities, and meditative concentrations, he could never sit at the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Regarding this, it is said: 27.

Just as the world, including the gods, might perform purification for a piece of glass to make it appear like a *vaiḍūrya* gem, yet that glass will never truly become a *vaiḍūrya*, for its nature remains entirely different from that of a god—
even so it is with a disciple who, though endowed with morality, learning, meditation, and all virtuous qualities.
Having conquered Māra while seated at the seat of awakening and having touched awakening, he will become a Sugata.
KP.92 Just as, Kāśyapa, when the polishing of a great *vaiḍūrya* jewel is being performed, it becomes a source of income for many hundreds of thousands of *karṣāpaṇa* coins;
even so, Kāśyapa, when the cultivation of a bodhisattva is being performed, it becomes a source of income for many hundreds of thousands of *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.
Regarding this, it is said: 28.

Just as there is a great income from the refining of *karṣāpaṇa* coins when they are worked upon as *vaiḍūrya* gems, so too is the cultivation of the sons of the Buddha likewise the source of many disciples. (30)
KP.93 Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Mahākāśyapa once more:
"Kāśyapa, in whatever region there is one who is like a camel-smoke, black-headed and lying on his back, that region becomes beset by calamities, afflictions, and distresses.
But if, Kāśyapa, in whatever region there is a bodhisattva..."
That region becomes free from calamity, free from affliction, and free from distress.

Therefore, Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva should be one who is dedicated to the welfare of sentient beings; he should relinquish all his roots of merit for the sake of all sentient beings, and he should correctly and fully accomplish every root of merit.

And whoever seeks the medicine of knowledge should go in the four directions and perform genuine medical treatment for all sentient beings; by means of genuine medical treatment, sentient beings are to be healed. Kāśyapa, what is genuine medical treatment? Namely: impurity is the medical treatment for passion; loving-kindness is the medical treatment for hatred; and the contemplation of dependent origination is the medical treatment for delusion and for all types of views.

Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the remedy for all conceptual constructions, discursive thoughts, imaginings, mental engagements, and reflections; signlessness (*ānimitta*) is the remedy for the abandonment of the entire realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm; wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) is the remedy for all perversions; and the four remedies for the perversions are as follows: the remedy for the perception of permanence in the impermanent is the realization that "all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent."

The perception of pleasure in what is suffering is treated by the [remedy] that "all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are suffering"; the perception of "mine" in what is not mine is treated by the [remedy] that "all phenomena (*dharma*) are non-self (*anātman*); the perception of purity in what is impure is treated by the [remedy] that "Nirvana is peace. (KP.95) The four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are the remedies for those who rely on the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena: one dwells contemplating the body in the body, yet does not [abide] in the view of self regarding the contemplation of the body.
He falls away;
dwelling as one who contemplates feelings within feeling, he does not fall away from that contemplation of feeling through the occurrence of a view of self.
Dwelling as one who contemplates the mind within the mind, he does not fall away from that contemplation of the mind through the occurrence of a view of a living soul.
He dwells contemplating phenomena within phenomena, yet he does not fall into a view of a person regarding that contemplation of phenomena.
The four right efforts are the remedy for abandoning all unwholesome phenomena;
they lead to the complete fulfillment of all wholesome phenomena.
The four bases of psychic power lead to the relinquishing of the grasping at a solid mass of body and mind.
The five faculties and the five powers are the remedies for lack of faith, laziness, forgetfulness, mental distraction, lack of clear comprehension, and faulty wisdom.
The seven factors of enlightenment are the remedies for ignorance regarding the collection of phenomena. The noble eightfold path is the remedy for the faulty wisdom of all rival disputants.
"Kāśyapa, this is called the treatment for those who have entered upon wrong paths; this is called the true treatment. In this regard, Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva should apply himself to practice.
Kāśyapa, whatever physicians or medical students there may be in Jambudvīpa, among them all, Jīvaka is declared to be the foremost king of physicians.
Kāśyapa, even if all the sentient beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system were each like Jīvaka, the king of physicians, and they were all to ask [about this matter],"
"What is the medicine for one who is established in seen transgression and has fallen?
They were not capable, nor were they able to explain or point out that matter, nor was there any knower of such knowledge among them.
In this regard, Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva should investigate thus: "I must not be content with worldly medicine."

"I must seek the supramundane medicine of knowledge and correctly gather all roots of virtue. Thus should one reflect: "Having gathered that medicine of knowledge, I shall go in the four directions and provide true medical treatment for all sentient beings; and by means of this true medical treatment, sentient beings are to be healed."
KP.97. In that regard, what is the supramundane medicinal knowledge?

It is this: the knowledge of causes and conditions; the knowledge of resolute conviction regarding phenomena that are selfless, devoid of a sentient being, devoid of a life-principle, devoid of a nourisher, and devoid of a person;
and the vigor for seeking out the mind without fear toward phenomena that are empty and non-apprehendable.
He thus searches for the mind:
"Which mind is it that becomes lustful, or hateful, or deluded?
Is it past, future, or present?"
If the past mind has already ceased, and if the future mind has not yet arrived, then there is no abiding of the present mind.
Kāśyapa, for the mind is not apprehended externally, nor internally, nor in between the two. KP.98

For the mind, Kāśyapa, is formless, invisible, non-obstructive, non-manifest, non-communicative, non-abiding, and homeless. For the mind, Kāśyapa, has not been seen by all the Buddhas, they do not see it, they will not see it, and they shall not see it.
Since it has not been seen by all the Buddhas, is not seen, and will not be seen, how can its movement be perceived?

Dharmas do not proceed otherwise than through a continuum fallen into false inversion. For, Kāśyapa, the mind is like an illusion; having conceptualized what is unreal, it grasps at various rebirths. For, Kāśyapa, the mind is like the wind:
far-reaching, ungraspable, and without movement. For, Kāśyapa, the mind is like the current of a river: unstable and ever-arising.

“Kāśyapa, the broken and dissolved mind is indeed like the flame of a lamp; it proceeds by way of causes and conditions. Kāśyapa, the mind is indeed like lightning; it is momentary, perishing in an instant, and unstable.
Kāśyapa, the mind is indeed like space; it is defiled by adventitious secondary afflictions. Kāśyapa, the mind is indeed like a monkey.”
“Kāśyapa, the mind is like a painter because it constructs various karmas through its attachment to sense objects.

Kāśyapa, the mind is unstable because it gives rise to various afflictions. Kāśyapa, the mind moves alone because it has no second companion. Kāśyapa, the mind is like a king because it exercises sovereignty over all phenomena.”
14. For the mind, Kāśyapa, is like an enemy, because it gives rise to all suffering.

15. For the mind, Kāśyapa, is like a house of sand, because of the perception of permanence in the impermanent. 16. For the mind, Kāśyapa, is like a blue fly, because of the perception of purity in the impure. 17. For the mind, Kāśyapa, is like a fishhook, because of suffering.

“Kāśyapa, the mind is like a dream because of the perception of pleasure. Kāśyapa, the mind is like an enemy because of the perception of ‘mine’ toward what is not one’s own, due to its performing various kinds of harmful actions. Kāśyapa, the mind is like a *yakṣa* that feeds on vital energy, because it is always seeking an opportunity for entry. Kāśyapa, the mind is like an adversary, because it is always seeking out vulnerabilities.”

KP.101 "For the mind, Kāśyapa, is always rising and falling, afflicted by attachment and aversion. 23. For the mind, Kāśyapa, is like a thief, because it steals all roots of merit. 24. For the mind, Kāśyapa, delights in forms, being like the eye of a courtesan.
25. For the mind, Kāśyapa, delights in sounds, being like the war drum. 26. For the mind, Kāśyapa, always delights in fragrances."

"Kāśyapa, the mind is like a boar in a corpse; for the mind, Kāśyapa, delights in flavors, being like a servant-girl who eats flavorful food. Kāśyapa, the mind delights in tactile sensations, like a fly in a vessel of oil.
Kāśyapa, when the mind is thoroughly sought after, it is not found. That which is not found is not apprehended; that which is not apprehended is neither past, nor future, nor present."
That which is neither past, nor future, nor present has transcended the [three] times; that which has transcended the three times neither exists nor does not exist.
That which neither exists nor does not exist—[is it not thus?]
That which is unborn is not born;
that which is not born has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); that which has no intrinsic nature has no arising;
that which has no arising has no cessation; and that which has no cessation has no passing away.

There is no departure from it, no going, no coming, no passing away, and no rebirth. Where there is no going, no coming, no passing away, and no rebirth, there are no conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). Where there are no conditioned phenomena, that is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); that is the lineage (*gotra*) of the noble ones (*ārya*).

KP.103: That which is the lineage (*gotra*) of the noble ones (*ārya*) is where there is neither training (*śikṣā*) nor reliance (*niśraya*), nor non-reliance (*aniśraya*). Where there is neither training nor reliance nor non-reliance, there is no transgression of the training (*śikṣāvyatikrama*). Where there is no transgression of the training, there is neither restraint (*saṃvara*) nor non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). Where there is neither restraint nor non-restraint...

Therein there is no movement, no conduct, and no activity; where there is no movement, no conduct, and no activity, there is neither mind nor mental factors; where there is neither mind nor mental factors, there is neither mind-organ nor consciousness;
where there is neither mind-organ nor consciousness—
In that state there is neither action nor ripening; where there is neither action nor ripening, there is neither pleasure nor pain.

That which is neither pleasure nor pain is the lineage (*gotra*) of the noble ones (*ārya*). In that lineage of the noble ones, there is neither action nor the formative impulse of action (*karmābhisaṃskāra*);
furthermore, in that lineage no action is performed by body, nor by speech, nor by mind.
Furthermore, within that lineage there is no establishment of inferior, superior, or middling; that lineage is equal, because it is equal to space.
That lineage is without distinction, because all phenomena have a single flavor.
That lineage is secluded, because of the seclusion of body and mind. (KP.104)
That lineage is in accordance with *nirvāṇa*.

That lineage is stainless, being free from the defilement of all afflictions. That lineage is selfless, being free from the notions of "I" and "mine. That lineage is non-dual, having emerged through the equality of the real and the unreal. That lineage is truth, by virtue of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
That lineage is inexhaustible because it is ultimately unarisen;
that lineage is eternal because it is always the suchness of phenomena;
that lineage is auspicious because it has nirvana as its supreme goal.
That lineage is auspicious, being free from stains of every kind;
that lineage is selfless, because when the self is thoroughly sought, it is not found;
that lineage is pure, due to its ultimate purity.

“Kāśyapa, search within; do not run outside. For what reason? Kāśyapa, in the future there will be monks who are like dogs chasing after a clod of earth. And how, Kāśyapa, are monks like dogs chasing after a clod of earth? It is just as if, Kāśyapa, a dog frightened by a clod of earth chases after that very clod.”
It does not pursue the one by whom that clod was thrown.
In the same way, Kāśyapa, there are some ascetics and brahmins who, terrified by forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles, dwell in forest retreats.
While they are there, alone and without a second, dwelling in physical seclusion, attractive objects—forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles—arise before them.
Being observers of those, they dwell devoted to the pursuit of pleasant pleasures.
They do not know, nor do they understand, what the escape from forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles is.

Being ignorant and lacking understanding, they have entered among villages, towns, market towns, hamlets, and royal capitals, yet they do not comprehend the taste, the disadvantage, and the escape regarding those forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles; and if, having gone to the forest, they should pass away while still craving other forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles.
For those who abide in worldly restraint, rebirth occurs in the heavenly world;
there too, they are struck by the five divine qualities of sensual pleasure.

Having passed away from there, being still unliberated, they fall into the four states of woe—namely, the hells, the animal realm, the world of Yama, and the asuras. Thus, Kāśyapa, monks are like dogs chasing after clods of earth.
And how, Kāśyapa, is a monk not like a dog chasing after a clod of earth? Kāśyapa, it is when a monk, when reviled, does not revile in return; when struck, does not strike back;
when scolded, does not scold in return; and when insulted, does not insult in return.
When provoked to anger, he does not respond with anger;
he inwardly reflects upon the state of his own mind, asking:
"Who is it that reviles or strikes?"
Whether reviled, scolded, or provoked to anger—
in this way, Kāśyapa, a monk does not become like one who chases after a dog’s clod, nor does he become like a house.
Regarding this, it is said:
Just as a dog, being frightened by a clod of earth, runs after the clod and not toward the person who threw it,
so too are some ascetics or brahmins here.
Fearing forms and the like, they took refuge in dwelling in the forest;
and while they were living there in the wilderness, forms and the other [objects] became desirable to them upon being seen.
Lacking higher knowledge regarding the state of internal equanimity,
and not understanding its danger or the escape from it, she has returned once more to rely upon the village.
Furthermore, being tormented by forms,
some fall away from the gods and humans;
even there, having enjoyed divine pleasures, they [fall].
Some fall into the states of woe; having died again and again, the deluded undergo suffering.
Thus, indeed, they are bound by hundreds of miseries and have been taught by the Sugata to be like dogs and clods of earth.
When reviled, they do not revile in return; likewise, when struck or censured, some do not censure in turn.
One who is not reviled does not revile others in return; one who is not provoked to anger does not provoke anger in others, being gentle.
Examining the internal mind, he seeks tranquility and possesses mindfulness.
One endowed with such moral conduct and vows is not described by the Jina as being equal to a dog.
KP.108: "Kāśyapa, it is just as if, for example, there were a skilled horse-trainer's son;
wherever on the ground a horse stumbles, or rears up, or performs the act of kicking."
And in each and every such place on the earth, he restrains it; he restrains it in such a way that it does not become agitated again.
In the very same way, Kāśyapa, wherever a monk who is a practitioner of yoga perceives a transformation of the mind, there and then he applies himself to its restraint.
He restrains the mind in such a way that it does not become agitated again; regarding this, it is said:
Just as a skilled horse-trainer restrains a stumbling horse,
so too the yogi, seeing a transformation of the mind, restrains it in such a way that it does not become agitated.
Kāśyapa, it is just as, for example, a throat-spasm seizes all the sense faculties and functions to obstruct the life-faculty;
even so, Kāśyapa, the grasping at a self among all views functions to obstruct the life-faculty of the Dharma. Regarding this, it is said:
Just as a throat-seizure (galagraha) restrains the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) and grants no happiness,
so too does the view of self (ātmadṛṣṭi) among those who hold views destroy this life of the Dharma.
KP.110 Just as, Kāśyapa, wherever a person is bound, he must be liberated from that very place;
even so, Kāśyapa, wherever the mind becomes attached, it must be liberated from that very place.
In this regard, the following is said:
Just as a man who is bound must be released from every side, so too the deluded mind of a yogin must be liberated from whatever it becomes attached to.
KP.111: "Kāśyapa, there are these two things that obstruct the sky for one who has gone forth.
Which two?
The pursuit of Lokāyata mantras and..."
And by way of carrying an overflowing alms-bowl and robes—
these two. Regarding this, the following is said:

Diligent application to the study of Lokāyata and the constant wearing of robes and bowl for the sake of gaining a reputation for spiritual realization— these two things are established [as obstacles] and should be avoided by a bodhisattva.
KP.112: "Kāśyapa, there are these two firm bonds for one who has gone forth.

What are the two? Namely, the bond created by the view of a self and the bond of gain, honor, and praise. These, Kāśyapa, are the two firm bonds for one who has gone forth. Regarding this, it is said: (Verse 2)
