There are two firm bonds for one who has gone forth: the bond of speculative views has been declared by the Buddhas to be the first, and the bond of honor, gain, and fame is the second; these should always be abandoned by one who has gone forth.
KP.113: "Kāśyapa, there are these two things that create obstacles for one who has gone forth.
Which two?
Associating with the faction of householders and hostility toward the faction of the noble ones. These two, Kāśyapa, are the things that create obstacles for one who has gone forth."
In this regard, the following is said: 3.
Devotion to the side of householders and disparagement of the side of teachers—
these two obstacles, which act as hindrances, should be avoided by a bodhisattva.
KP.114: "Kāśyapa, there are these two stains of one who has gone forth. What are the two?

Namely, the habituation to the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the attachment to frequenting the families of friends and the families from which one begs for alms. These, Kāśyapa, are the two stains of one who has gone forth. Regarding this, it is said: 4. "Kāśyapa, there are these two stains of one who has gone forth. What are the two? Namely, the habituation to the afflictions and the attachment to frequenting the families of friends and the families from which one begs for alms. These, Kāśyapa, are the two stains of one who has gone forth. Regarding this, it is said:

If one who has gone forth should harbor afflictions and cultivate friendship with a family that lives on alms, these two are indeed taught by the Lord of Jinas to be stains; they are to be avoided by a bodhisattva.
KP.115. Kāśyapa, there are these two thunderbolts that fall upon one who has gone forth. Which two?

The rejection of the true Dharma and the consumption of what has been given out of faith by one whose ethical discipline has lapsed. These, Kāśyapa, are the two dharmas that are like thunderbolts falling upon one who has gone forth. Regarding this, it is said: 5. Kāśyapa, these two are like a thunderbolt falling upon a renunciant. What are the two? They are the rejection of the true Dharma and the enjoyment of gifts given in faith by one who has fallen away from moral conduct. These, Kāśyapa, are the two things for a renunciant that are like a thunderbolt’s strike. On this point, the following is said:
The rejection of the true Dharma and the feeding of one who has fallen from moral conduct—these two are like the falling of a thunderbolt; they should be avoided by those who are sons of kings.
KP.116: "Kāśyapa, there are these two wounds of one who has gone forth. Which two?
Scrutinizing the faults of others and concealing one's own faults. These, Kāśyapa, are the two wounds of one who has gone forth. Regarding this, it is said: (Verse 16)
One who conceals his own faults and observes only the faults of others—
these two types of persons, who are like poison and fire, should be avoided by the discerning.
KP.117: "Kāśyapa, there are these two torments for one who has gone forth. What are the two?

Namely, wearing the saffron robe while still being stained by passions, and accepting service and attendance from those who possess virtue and moral discipline. These, Kāśyapa, are the two torments for one who has gone forth.
Regarding this, it is said: (Verse 7)
For one whose mind is possessed of passion, wearing the saffron robe and associating with those endowed with virtue—serving, attending upon, and saluting them—these two things are to be avoided.

KP.118. “Kāśyapa, there are these two long-term ailments of one who has gone forth. Which two? They are: the mental fixation of one who is conceited, and the discouragement of beings who have set out in the Mahāyāna. These two, Kāśyapa, are the long-term ailments of one who has gone forth.
Regarding this, it is said: 18.”
The mental composure of those who are conceited, and the turning away from the Buddha-vehicle—
these two, indeed, are said by the Jina, the peerless one, to be the failings of one who has gone forth.
KP.119: "Kāśyapa, there are these two incurable ailments of one who has gone forth.
Which two?
Namely, the repeated committing of offenses and the failure to acknowledge them."
And lack of resolve—these two, Kāśyapa, are incurable ailments for one who has gone forth. 9.
KP.120: "Kāśyapa, there are these two thorns for one who has gone forth. What are the two?
Namely, the transgression of the training rules and passing away without having extracted the essence. These, Kāśyapa, are the two thorns for one who has gone forth."
KP.121: "O Kāśyapa, 'ascetic, ascetic'—thus it is said.
To what extent, Kāśyapa, is one called an ascetic?
There are these four types of ascetics, Kāśyapa. What are the four? Namely, the ascetic by way of complexion, form, marks, and appearance."

“Kāśyapa, there are these four kinds of śramaṇas: the śramaṇa who is a hypocrite concealing his conduct, the śramaṇa who is a śramaṇa for the sake of fame, reputation, and praise, and the śramaṇa of genuine practice.
Kāśyapa, among these, who is the śramaṇa who possesses [only] appearance, form, marks, and shape? Here, Kāśyapa, a certain śramaṇa is endowed with appearance, form, marks, and shape.”

Wrapped in the saṅghāṭī robe, with a shaven head and a proper bowl held in hand, he nevertheless possesses an impure practice of bodily action, an impure practice of vocal action, and an impure practice of mental action. He is undisciplined, unliberated, untamed, unpeaceful, unguarded, and undisciplined; he is greedy, lazy, and practices the conduct of immoral and evil dharmas. Kāśyapa, this is called a śramaṇa by virtue of his complexion, form, marks, and appearance.

KP.123. In this regard, Kāśyapa, who is the śramaṇa who is a hypocrite regarding the concealment of conduct? Here, Kāśyapa, a certain śramaṇa is endowed with proper conduct and behavior; he moves with clear comprehension through the four modes of deportment; he eats coarse food and drink; he is content with the four noble lineages; he is unmixed with householders or renunciants; he speaks little and utters few words; and such are his modes of deportment.
They are fabricated through hypocrisy and flattery;
they do not lead to the purification of the mind,
nor to tranquility, nor to complete peace.
He is not for self-control;
he holds the view of apprehension,
and having heard that all phenomena are empty and non-apprehensible, he perceives them as a precipice.
And toward those monks who are proponents of emptiness, he conceives a thought of lack of faith; this, Kāśyapa, is called the "hypocritical ascetic who conceals his conduct."

KP.124. In this regard, Kāśyapa, what is the ascetic who seeks fame, reputation, and praise? Here, Kāśyapa, a certain ascetic guards his moral discipline after careful reflection, thinking: "How might others know me to be virtuous?
He acquires learning after careful reflection, thinking: "How might others know me to be one of great erudition?"
He dwells in the forest with deliberate intention, thinking:
"How may others know me as a forest-dweller?
With deliberate intention, he dwells with few desires, contented, and secluded.
It is merely for the sake of showing off to others, and not for disenchantment, nor for dispassion, nor for cessation, nor for peace, nor for full awakening,
nor for the state of a śramaṇa.
Not for the sake of being a brahmin,
nor for the sake of nirvāṇa;
this, Kāśyapa, is called the śramaṇa of fame, renown, and verses.

KP.125. In this regard, Kāśyapa, who is the śramaṇa of true practice? Kāśyapa, it is that monk who has no desire even for his body or his life, let alone for gain, honor, or fame. Having heard the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, he becomes satisfied in mind; established in suchness, he practices the holy life (brahmacarya) without even desiring nirvāṇa.
How much more so, then, would one who has no interest even in the view of emptiness due to delighting in the three realms?
How much more so, then, would one have no interest in the views of a self, a sentient being, a living soul, a nourisher, or a person?
Furthermore, such a person relies upon the Dharma.
He seeks liberation from the afflictions within himself and does not run outward; seeing that all phenomena are by nature utterly pure and undefiled,
he becomes an island unto himself with no other island, and even in terms of the Dharma he does not perceive the Tathāgata, let alone in his form-body.
Even from the perspective of detachment, one does not adhere to the Dharma, let alone express it through the path of speech.

One does not even conceptualize the unconditioned Noble Saṅgha, let alone by way of gathering in a group. Nor is one intent upon the abandoning of any phenomenon, nor its cultivation, nor its realization.
He does not grow within saṃsāra; he does not delight in nirvāṇa;
he does not seek liberation.
There is no bondage;
having realized that all phenomena are by nature parinirvāṇized, one neither wanders in saṃsāra nor passes into parinirvāṇa. Kāśyapa, this is called the śramaṇa who practices according to reality.
"Kāśyapa, one should apply oneself to the state of a recluse through the practice of reality; one must not be one who is a recluse in name only. These, Kāśyapa, are the four types of recluses.
Regarding this, it is said:"

KP.126 One who is impure in body, speech, and mind, undisciplined, unguarded, and unrestrained; greedy, though shaven-headed, with robes and bowl in hand, and possessing the outward form and marks of a *śramaṇa*—
even if endowed with proper conduct and practice, yet eating coarse food and indulging in hypocrisy and the like.
Even though endowed with the four noble lineages, he completely avoids social contact; yet all those [associations] lead him neither to self-control, nor to peace, nor even to world-weariness.
Perceiving emptiness and signlessness as a precipice, his conduct is guarded and his second [nature] is deceitful.
The ascetic qualities, ethical discipline, learning, and meditative concentration serve as causes for inspiring confidence in others;

they do not lead to peace nor to world-weariness. This is the third type of śramaṇa, who is devoted to fame and reputation. (4) But he who seeks neither body nor life, and who turns his back on gain and honor—[he is the true one].
Having heard of liberation as the gateway to arising, they have no desire for any state of existence within the realms of becoming. 5 //
Examine all phenomena as absolutely empty; one perceives neither nirvāṇa nor non-nirvāṇa.
Always observing phenomena through dispassion, one who has attained nirvāṇa sees the unconditioned phenomenon as impermanent.
KP.127 "Kāśyapa, it is just as if a poor man were to have the name 'Wealthy Treasury.
What do you think, Kāśyapa, would that name be appropriate for that poor man?
He replied, "Certainly not, Blessed Lord."
The Blessed One said:
"In the same way, Kāśyapa, those who are called 'śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas' do not actually possess the qualities of a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa."
I call those "poor men.
Regarding this, it is said:
Just as the name of a poor man would not be fitting even in a wealthy treasury, so too [is the name of the Buddha inappropriate for them].
A śramaṇa devoid of the qualities of a śramaṇa does not shine, like a poor man who is called "wealthy."
KP.128 "Kāśyapa, it is just as if some man, being carried away by a great ocean of water, were to die of thirst.

In the very same way, Kāśyapa, there are certain recluses and brahmins here who master many teachings, yet they do not dispel the thirst of passion; they are unable to dispel the thirst of hatred or the thirst of delusion."
Being carried away by that great ocean of Dharma, they pass away with the thirst of the afflictions and become destined for the miserable realms.
Regarding this, it is said: 2.
Just as a person being carried away by a flood of water might die of thirst,
so too those who recite many teachings, while remaining in the ocean of Dharma, go to a state of woe through their craving for the Dharma.
Kāśyapa, it is just as if a physician, having taken up a load of medicinal herbs, were to wander about, yet some illness should arise within him that he is unable to treat.

In the same way, Kāśyapa, the affliction of the defilements (*kleśavyādhi*) of one who is learned (*bahuśruta*) should be viewed: if he is unable to treat his own affliction by means of that learning, that learning of his will be useless.
In this regard, the following is said: 3.

Just as a physician, though possessing a store of medicines, might wander throughout the entire world yet fail to cure those afflicted by disease— his [medical knowledge] would indeed be rendered useless; so too a monk, though endowed with the virtues of moral discipline and possessed of scriptural learning, does not provide treatment.
The pain arising from afflictions through improper mental application is in vain; his exertion in study is merely labor spent.
Kāśyapa, it is just as if a sick man worthy of a king’s medicine were to die because of a lack of restraint while using that medicine.
In the same way, Kāśyapa, the afflictions of one who is learned should be viewed as a disease; he dies because of that lack of restraint.
If a king, having procured medicines worthy of a king, goes to the states of woe due to a lack of restraint, regarding this it is said: 4.

Just as a man who has drunk a medicine fit for a king might suffer a fall despite his self-restraint, so too does this disease of the afflictions cause one who is learned to meet his end here through his very restraint. Kāśyapa, it is just as if a priceless great Vaiḍūrya jewel were to fall into excrement and become useless for its intended purpose.
In the same way, Kāśyapa, the fall from gain and honor of one who is learned should be seen as being like falling into excrement;
he becomes destitute among gods and humans.
Regarding this, it is said: 5.
"Just as a jewel that has fallen into filth becomes loathsome and is no longer as it was before,
I say, O monk, that even for a monk of great learning, the fall from honor is exactly like that.
It is just as if, Kāśyapa, that very same great Vaiḍūrya gem were to be pulled out from a heap of impure refuse, washed, thoroughly rinsed, and well-polished."

Just as that [jewel] does not abandon its very nature as a precious gem, even so, Kāśyapa, one who is well-learned purifies all afflictions with little effort and does not abandon his very nature as a jewel of great wisdom. Kāśyapa, it is just as if there were a golden garland upon the head of a corpse;
even so, Kāśyapa, should the wearing of the saffron robe by one of immoral conduct be regarded.
In this regard, the following is said: 7.
Just as a golden garland placed upon the head of a corpse would be like a flower wreath [of no value], so too,
seeing those of immoral conduct wearing saffron robes, one should not harbor mental aversion toward them.

Kāśyapa, it is just as if, for example, a son of a merchant or a prince—purely dressed and anointed with excellent sandalwood paste—were to have a garland of campaka flowers bound upon his head. In the same way, the wearing of the saffron robe by one who is thus [pure] and possessed of great learning is to be viewed. Regarding this, it is said: 8.
Just as the beautiful, fragrant, and delightful garland of *campaka* flowers adorns the son of a guild-leader who has bathed and anointed himself,
even so does the saffron robe adorn one who abides in restraint and is possessed of great learning.
One should look for one who is endowed with ethical discipline, [and] possessed of virtues. 2.
KP.134. “Kāśyapa, there are these four who are immoral yet resemble those possessed of morality. What are the four? Here, Kāśyapa, a certain monk dwells restrained by the restraint of the Prātimokṣa;
he is perfected in conduct and resort, sees danger in even the slightest faults, and trains himself in the precepts of training.”
He dwells endowed with completely pure actions of body, speech, and mind;
he is pure in livelihood, and he is one who speaks of a self—Kāśyapa, this is the first person who is immoral and should be regarded as a counterfeit of one who possesses morality.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, suppose here a certain monk is a holder of the Vinaya;

he applies the discipline and is established in the protection of the Vinaya, yet his view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) has not been displaced. This, Kāśyapa, is the second type of one who is immoral and a mere counterfeit of one who possesses morality.

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, suppose here a certain monk dwells in loving-kindness toward sentient beings... [and] is endowed with [this quality], yet having heard that all phenomena are unborn, he is terrified, he trembles,
and he falls into a state of dread.
This, Kāśyapa, is the third type of immoral person who is a mere counterfeit of one possessed of morality.

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, here a certain monk may possess the twelve ascetic qualities (*dhutaguṇa*), yet he holds views of objective apprehension (*upalambhadṛṣṭi*) and remains established in the conceit of "I" (*ahaṅkāra*). Kāśyapa, this is the fourth type of immoral person; these four should be understood as those who resemble those possessing ethical discipline (*śīlavantapratirūpaka*).

KP.135: "O Kāśyapa, that which is called 'discipline, discipline' is where there is no self... no 'mine,' no sentient being, no designation of a sentient being, no action, no non-action, no doing, and no non-doing."
It is neither conduct nor non-conduct, neither movement nor non-movement; it is neither name nor form, neither sign nor signlessness;
it is neither tranquility nor lack of tranquility, neither grasping nor relinquishing, neither the graspable nor the ungraspable.

There is no sentient being, nor the designation of a sentient being; no speech, nor the designation of speech; no mind, nor the designation of mind; no world, nor non-world; no reliance, nor non-reliance; no exalting of one's own morality, no disparaging of the poor morality of others, and no conceit regarding morality.
There is no conceptualization of ethical discipline, no discrimination, no volitional construction, and no thorough conceptualization.

This, Kāśyapa, is called the ethical discipline of the noble ones: it is untainted, not included within the three realms, does not follow after the triple world, and is free from all dependencies. At that time, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
For one possessed of virtue, there is no "m... [of self], nothing whatsoever,
no pride, no dependence,
no darkness, and no bondage.
For one possessed of virtue there is no dust, no...
[defilement]; he is peaceful, thoroughly calmed, with a mind stilled, free from conceptual construction, devoid of discrimination, and without affliction.
Completely liberated from the conceit of "I" and "mine," O Śikṣin Kāśyapa, one does not look after the body nor seek after life within the teaching of the Buddha.
One who is indifferent to all rebirths in existence,
who has gone rightly, and who is established in the [Dharma]— he, Kāśyapa, is virtuous in the teaching of the Buddha. 3.
Neither smeared by the world nor dependent on the world, having attained illumination, free from "mine-ness" and without grasping;
he has no perception of a self, nor does he have a perception of others.
Having fully understood perception, his ethical conduct is purified;
for him there is neither the near shore nor the far shore,
and he is never attached to either the near or the far shore.
Free from attachment, without deceit, and without outflows—
such a person, Kāśyapa, is virtuous in the teaching of the Buddha.
With a mind unattached to name and form, he is indeed composed and has a well-tamed heart.
He whose self here [is not attached] and who does not regard anything as belonging to a self—by this much he is said to be established in ethical discipline (śīla).
He does not take pride in the Prātimokṣa training, nor does he become absorbed in it here.
Furthermore, he seeks the Noble Path; these are the signs of one whose ethical discipline is purified.
One who is not supreme in ethical discipline nor absorbed in meditative concentration does not seek further the cultivation of wisdom.
This non-apprehension is the noble lineage, pure ethical discipline, praised by the Sugatas;
for one whose mind is liberated from the view of a self-identity, there arises here no sense of "I" or "mine."
One is resolved upon the sphere of the Buddhas, which is emptiness; there exists nothing equal to this morality.
(9) Established in morality, concentration becomes pure; for one who has attained concentration, there is the cultivation of wisdom.
Through wisdom, knowledge becomes purified, and for one whose knowledge is purified, there is the perfection of morality. (10)
Furthermore, while this exposition of verses was being spoken, the minds of eight hundred bhikṣus were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging;
and the dust-free, stainless Dharma-eye regarding phenomena was purified in thirty-two thousand beings.
Five hundred bhikṣus who had attained meditative concentration rose from their seats and departed, for they could not enter into, penetrate, or have faith in this profound teaching of the Dharma.

KP.139 Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, these five hundred monks who have attained meditative concentration, having risen from their seats, have departed; they do not enter into, do not plunge into, and do not have faith in this profound teaching of the Dharma. The Blessed One said:
"It is because, Kāśyapa, these monks are free from conceit and do not have faith in this profound production of verses."
Having heard this teaching on the purity of untainted ethical discipline, they do not enter into it, do not have faith in it, and do not penetrate it. For what reason?

Because, Kāśyapa, this formulation of verses is profound; the awakening of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is profound. It is impossible for beings who have not planted roots of merit, who are gripped by the fear of evil, and who abound in a lack of faith, to have faith in it.
or to examine, or to penetrate it.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, these five hundred monks were formerly disciples of other sects during the teaching of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha Kāśyapa.
Having heard a single discourse on the Dharma from the presence of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, they heard it again and again with the intention of finding fault.
And they attained clarity of mind, thinking, "How wonderful! This Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, is indeed so sweet and pleasing.
Having passed away from there, through that single moment of clarity of mind, they died and were reborn among the Trāyastriṃśa gods. Not even...
Kāśyapa, these five hundred monks who have gone forth here in my teaching under such causes have fallen into wrong views;
they do not enter into, do not plunge into, do not resolve upon, and do not have faith in this profound teaching of the Dharma.
However, they have already performed the preparatory work for this teaching of the Dharma, and they shall no longer fall into states of ruin.
They will attain final nirvana by means of these very aggregates.
KP.141 Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the venerable Subhūti: "Go, Subhūti, and instruct these monks. Subhūti said:
"Even the words spoken by the Blessed One himself these monks oppose; what need is there to mention my own?"
Then, at that time, the Blessed One created two monks on the very path by which those monks were traveling. Thereupon,
those five hundred monks approached the place where those two created monks were, and having approached them, they spoke as follows:

"Venerable sirs, where will you go? They replied, "We shall go to forest retreats; we shall dwell there in comfort and ease. For what reason? Because we do not approve of, nor do we penetrate, that teaching of the Dharma which the Blessed One teaches."
We do not have faith;
we are terrified, we are trembling, and we fall into a state of panic.
Therefore, let us two dwell happily in forest retreats.
KP.142 Those five hundred monks also said this:

"Venerable sirs, we too do not enter into, do not plunge into, and do not have faith in the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dharma; we are terrified, we are trembling, and we fall into a state of panic."

"We shall dwell in forest hermitages, abiding in the bliss of meditative concentration. The two emanated monks said, "Venerable sirs, we shall recite together and not dispute; for non-dispute is the supreme quality of a śramaṇa.
What is here called 'nirvāṇa,' venerable sirs?"
What is that dharma which will attain parinirvāṇa? Furthermore, is there in this body any self,
or a sentient being, or a living soul, or a creature, or a person, or an individual, or a human, or a youth, or a doer,
or a maker, or an experiencer, or a knower, or a perceiver, or an arouser, or an originator who will attain parinirvāṇa?

KP.143 They said: "...Nowhere does it exist; in this body there is no self (ātman), nor a sentient being (sattva), nor a living soul (jīva), nor a creature (jantu), nor a person (puruṣa), nor an individual (pudgala), nor a human (manuja), nor a youth (mānava), nor an agent (kartṛ), nor a doer (kāraka), nor an experiencer (vedaka), nor a knower (jñātṛ), nor a perceiver (saṃjñātṛ), nor an arouser (utthāpaka) who will attain parinirvāṇa."
The emanated beings said,
"He will attain parinirvāṇa through further realization.
They replied, "Venerable ones, parinirvāṇa consists in the destruction of passion, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion."
The emanated beings asked: "Furthermore, Venerable Ones, do passion, hatred, and delusion exist such that you would exhaust them?
They replied:
"They are not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two."
"Nor do they arise as unimagined," the two emanated beings said.

"Therefore, venerable sirs, do not imagine us; do not conceptualize us. When, venerable sirs, you do not imagine and do not conceptualize, then, venerable sirs, you will neither be stained nor be discolored. And whoever, venerable sirs, does not..."
One who is neither attached nor detached... is said to be "peaceful" (KP 144).

"Venerable ones, ethical discipline does not transmigrate and does not pass into final nirvāṇa; concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, venerable ones, do not transmigrate and do not pass into final nirvāṇa. It is by means of these very dharmas, venerable ones, that nirvāṇa is indicated."

And these phenomena are empty, secluded, and ungraspable... O Venerable Ones, abandon that perception, namely, "this is parinirvāṇa. Do not form a perception of a perception; do not [form a perception] of a non-perception...
and through perception, fully understand perception.
He who fully understands perception through perception—that itself becomes his bondage to perception.

... Venerable ones, enter the attainment of the cessation of feeling and perception; do not conceptualize, do not proliferate. For a monk who has entered the attainment of the cessation of feeling and perception, there is nothing further.
"We say that this is what must be done.
While this Dharma discourse was being spoken, the minds of those five hundred monks were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging.
With their minds thus liberated, they approached the Blessed One; having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Then the Venerable Subhūti said this to those bodhisattvas:
"Where indeed, venerable ones, have you gone, or from where have you come? They replied: "Not for the sake of going anywhere, nor for the sake of coming from anywhere."
"Venerable Subhūti, the Dharma has been taught by the Blessed One. Subhūti said:
"Who, venerable sirs, is the Teacher?
They replied: "He who has arisen... will enter parinirvāṇa."
KP.146 Subhūti said: "Whose disciples are you? From whom have you been trained? They replied: "By one who has neither attained nor realized... Subhūti said: "From whom have you heard the Dharma?"
They said: "For whom there are no aggregates, no elements, and no sense-bases. Subhūti asked: "How then have you heard the Dharma?
They replied: "Neither for the sake of bondage nor for the sake of liberation."
Subhūti said:
"How have you been instructed? They replied:
"Neither for the sake of yoga nor for the sake of application."
"Not for the sake of abandonment.
Subhūti asked, "By whom have you been trained? They replied, "By him for whom there is no perfection of body and no activity of mind.
Subhūti said:
"How are you practicing so as to be liberated? They replied: "Neither for the destruction of ignorance, nor for the production of knowledge. (KP.147) Subhūti said:
"Whose disciples are you? They replied: "Of him who has neither attained nor [realized]... the perfectly awakened one. Subhūti said:

"How long will it be before you attain parinirvāṇa? They replied, "As long as it takes for the emanations of the Tathāgata to attain parinirvāṇa, so long will we attain parinirvāṇa. Subhūti said, "Have you accomplished your own welfare? They replied, "Because no objective entity is to be apprehended. Subhūti said:
"What was to be done has been accomplished by you.
They replied,
"Because the agent is unapprehendable..."
Subhūti said,
"Who are your fellow practitioners of the holy life?
They replied:
Those who do not engage in the three realms, nor move about [within them]... Subhūti said:

"Have your afflictions been exhausted? They replied, "Because all phenomena are ultimately exhausted. Subhūti said, "Have you conquered Māra? They replied, "Because the Māra of the aggregates is not to be found.
Subhūti said:

“Has the Tathāgata been served by you? They replied, “Neither by body nor by mind. Subhūti said, “Have you established yourselves on the ground of those worthy of offerings? They replied, “Because of non-grasping and because of non-clinging. Subhūti said, “Have you cut off saṃsāra?”
They said: "Because of being neither annihilated nor eternal. Subhūti said:
"Have you entered the stage of a śramaṇa?
They replied: "In the liberation that is unattached."
18. Subhūti said: "Where are you going, venerable sirs? They replied: "We go wherever the Tathāgata’s emanations go. 19.
KP.149 Thus, while the venerable Subhūti was questioning and those monks were responding,

in that assembly the minds of eight hundred monks and five hundred nuns were liberated through non-clinging. Furthermore, among thirty-two thousand beings— including gods and humans— the dust-free and stainless Dharma-eye regarding phenomena was purified.

KP.150 Then, indeed, the bodhisattva mahāsattva named Samantāloka said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva who wishes to train in the Dharma discourse of the Mahāratnakūṭa abide, and how should he practice?"
"How should one train... [the Buddha] said:

"Having taken up this Dharma-discourse, O son of good family, training has been proclaimed here for those true persons whose essence is practice; this Dharma-discourse will bring about the welfare of existence.
Just as if, O son of good family, some man were to board a boat made of clay, desiring to cross the river Gaṅgā."
What do you think, noble son? With what kind of vigor should that man steer the ship? [He replied: "With powerful vigor, Blessed One.
Why is that? Lest the ship should perish midway before I have reached the far shore;
lest this ship be shattered in the midst of this great ocean."
The Blessed One said:

"In this very way, Samantāloka, a bodhisattva must fully realize awakening with even greater strength and more powerful vigor; and with great power and vigor, the qualities of a Buddha must be fully realized."
KP.152 Thus, by way of non-attention: "Alas, this body is impermanent; it is composed of the four great elements, born from the *kalala* of mother and father.
It is unstable... not to be relied upon, subject to transformation, and characterized by being covered, bathed, massaged, broken, scattered, and destroyed.
It is moistened... nourished by months; it does not endure for long, and without food it cannot remain."

Worn out like a dilapidated house and weak, may it not happen that my death occurs before I have taken hold of [the Dharma]; for I have entered the great ocean of the flood, amidst beings who have encountered the four hundred and four diseases and are being carried away. Therefore, for the sake of delivering them, I shall fully prepare the great Dharma-ship of a Bodhisattva.
By means of this ship of Dharma, I shall ferry across all sentient beings who are being carried away by the ocean of saṃsāra and have not yet reached the shore.
Samantāloka, what kind of ship of Dharma should a bodhisattva assemble there?
Samantāloka, in this regard, a bodhisattva should assemble a ship of Dharma, namely, the equipment of a mind of universal equanimity.

They flow forth, accumulated through infinite merit, born from the fruit of ethical discipline (*śīla*), adorned with the ornaments of the retinue of generosity (*dāna*); they are firmly bound together by the solid essence of intention (*āśaya*), fastened with the nails of patience, gentleness, and mindfulness; they are constructed from the timber of the wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*) and firm vigor (*vīrya*), which constitute the equipment of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*); they are fashioned from the delightful workmanship of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and liberation; and they are perfectly completed through the skillful arts of the well-trained, peaceful, and noble ones.

It is of the nature of being absolutely unshakable, embraced by great compassion, and carried by the heroic steeds of the four means of attraction (*saṅgrahavastu*). It is well-guarded by the wisdom and knowledge that counteract adversaries; it is well-cultivated through skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*) and thoroughly purified by the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
It is brought forth by a body well-considered through the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Spreading forth through the right efforts, possessing the speed and swiftness of a thunderbolt,

well-observed by the faculties and free from crookedness in its giving, it has surged with the force of power; it is the awakening through the intermediate non-laxity of the factors of enlightenment, the abandoner of the path of Māra— the enemy and foe—
and the carrier of the sequence of pride, which abandons the fords of false teachers.

This great ship of Dharma has been described as characterized by calm abiding (*śamatha*) and directed toward the perfection of insight (*vipaśyanā*); it flows unattached between the two extremes. It is endowed with the causal dharmas, vast and expansive, possessing inexhaustible abandonment and freedom from bondage; its sound is proclaimed throughout the ten directions. As it approaches, approaching, it resounds with the cry: "Come, come! to those who take up this sound.
Leading to the city of Nirvana;
proceeding upon the path of security;
[possessing] great... wisdom; abandoning the view of a self-existent body.

O son of good family, such a Dharma... must be fully realized by a bodhisattva who, with a mind untiring for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of immeasurable eons, must ferry across all sentient beings by means of this ship of the True Dharma, for the sake of all sentient beings—[a ship] which goes to the further shore and is free from all minor views. KP.155.
Carried away by the four floods, O noble son, such beings must be gathered together by a Bodhisattva with a ship.
In that regard, what is the Bodhisattva’s universal light?
It is his application toward all sentient beings, which is unconditioned.
Intense aspiration through the purification of accumulation;

ardent vigor for the complete realization of all roots of merit; wholesome aspiration through appropriate mental attention; insatiability regarding what has been heard for the sake of fulfilling wisdom; and freedom from pride through the cultivation of wisdom.
Inclination toward the life of renunciation;
The pursuit of the Dharma is by way of relying on the ultimate meaning;
the pursuit of knowledge is by way of the meaning of ultimate pacification;
[the pursuit of] the Dharma... is by way of the meaning of non-arising.
The meaning of truth is by way of non-deceptiveness;
the meaning of emptiness is by way of correct application;
the meaning of seclusion is by way of ultimate... [cessation].
This, Samantāloka, is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s swift superknowledge.

KP.157 Then the venerable Mahākāśyapa said this to the Blessed One: “It is marvelous, Blessed One! It is marvelous, Sugata! To what extent this *Mahāratnakūṭa* sūtra is beneficial for sons of good family and daughters of good family who have set out in the Mahāyāna.”

"Blessed One, how much merit does that son of good family—or daughter of good family—generate who teaches even a single verse from this *Ratnakūṭa*, the king of sūtras? When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Mahākāśyapa: "Kāśyapa, as for that son of good family..."

Or if a son of noble family or a daughter of noble family were to take as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, break them down into atoms, and cast that many handfuls [of those atoms] into [the world-systems],
and having filled all those world-systems with [jewels], were to give them as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; [this would be the case].
And suppose one were to cause monasteries equal in number to the sands of the river Ganges to be built for as many Buddhas,

Blessed Ones, as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, and for each single Tathāgata; and suppose one were to serve, with provisions for comfort, the immeasurable community of disciples of each single Tathāgata among those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges.

And for as long as life lasts, he would provide service and attendance to those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, with agreeable deeds of body, speech, and mind; and having shattered as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges into atoms, or having had them shattered that many times over.

If one were to fill all those world-systems with the seven precious jewels and offer them to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and were to serve them throughout their entire lives with pleasing physical action, verbal action, and mental action— even if there were as many Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges...
One should honor, respect, and worship them, and for those who have entered final nirvāṇa,
one should cause stūpas made of the seven precious gems to be constructed.
And whichever son of good family or daughter of good family, from this *Mahāratnakūṭa*, the king of sūtras...
If one were to take up and retain even a single verse spoken by all the Buddhas, compared to this mass of merit,
that previous mass of merit does not approach even a hundredth part.
Even a thousandth part; who... even a thousandth part;
even a numerical fraction.
Not even a fraction,
not even a calculation,
not even a comparison.
Even compared to those who hear the *upaniṣads* and the *nakṣatra* [texts], and having heard them, do not reject them—
this person would generate a much greater mass of merit than they.
And whoever should hear, or cause to be written, or master this *Mātṛ...*— for him there shall never be a downfall;
that very [text] shall become his protection.

KP.160 And wherever this *Ratnakūṭa* Dharma-discourse is spoken, taught, written, or... or exists as a book, that spot of earth becomes a shrine for the world including the gods; and [it belongs] to whichever Dharma-preacher’s presence... it may be.

Whoever should hear, or take up, or write down, or master this Dharma-discourse, toward that Dharma-preacher such reverence should be generated as if toward the Tathāgata himself, Kāśyapa; and whoever honors, reveres, and respects that preacher of the Dharma... [will likewise honor the Tathāgata].
And at the time of his worship, he will have a vision of the Tathāgata.
Through that vision of the Tathāgata, he will attain ten purifications of bodily action. What are the ten?
Namely: he will die with a mind unconsumed by sensation.
There shall be no confusion of his vision; he shall not make a movement of his arms, nor shall he make a movement of his feet;
he shall not discharge excrement, nor shall he discharge urine.
6. He will not emit sweat;
7. he will not clench his fist;
8. nor will he touch the sky.
9 Just as when seated... [the rest of the verse]
